Godly and June

In a secluded monastery, a holy man named Godly lived. He had acquired a large sum of money by selling finely woven garments to the faithful. Godly trusted no one and kept his treasure close to him always.

A rogue named June, who stole money from others, observed Godly's treasure and thought: "How can I take this from him?" June couldn't break through the solid stone walls or enter the high door. He decided to win Godly's trust and become his disciple.

June approached Godly, bowed down, and said: "Glory to Shiva. Amen." He spoke with respect: "O holy sir, I see that life is short and fleeting. Delights are like a shadow. What should I do to safely cross the sea of life?" Godly was impressed by June's words.

Godly said: "You are blessed for being indifferent to the world at a young age. Saints are those who control their passions in youth. A holy sage's body may age, but their mind remains young." Godly then shared a prayer that could change one's caste and bring purity.

June listened and clasped Godly's feet. "Holy sir, please impose a vow on me." Godly agreed, but warned June not to enter his cell at night. June promised to follow the rules and take a vow.

As time passed, June served Godly, but Godly still did not trust him. He thought of killing Godly, but then a pupil's son arrived with an invitation for Godly to attend a ceremony. Godly took June along and, as they traveled, came to a river. He handed June his treasure and asked him to keep watch.

As soon as Godly was out of sight, June seized the treasure and ran away.

Leap and Creep

In a grand palace, a majestic bed stood, famous for its comfort and beauty. A plump and handsome louse named Creep lived on the bed's coverlet with her large family. She fed on the king's blood while he slept, growing stronger and healthier.

One day, a flea named Leap drifted in on the wind and landed on the bed. He was thrilled to see the luxurious coverlet, soft pillows, and sweet perfume. Leap was charmed by the bed's delightfulness and began to explore, eventually meeting Creep. She scolded him, "Where do you come from? This is a royal bed. Leave now and don't waste any more time."

Leap replied, "Madam, you shouldn't speak like that. As a guest, I deserve respect. I've tasted blood from various people, but this king's blood must be special. It's like nectar, free from impurities. I'd love to taste it and enjoy the pleasure and benefit."

Creep was taken aback by Leap's words. She remembered the story of a cunning prince who quoted a proverb to show respect to his guest. She agreed to let Leap stay, but with a condition: "When the king is drunk, tired, or asleep, then you may quietly bite him on the feet. That is the right time and place."

However, Leap misunderstood the condition and bit the king on the back when he was dozing off. The king was shocked and woke up, scratching his back and shouting for his servants to find the insect. Leap panicked and hid in a crevice, but the servants found Creep and her family, killing them instead.

The servants searched the bed, but Leap was nowhere to be found. They left, and the king was left with a painful scratch.

Moral: Being a good host means being mindful of your guests' needs and respecting their boundaries, lest you suffer the consequences.

The Old Man with the Young Wife

In a small town, a wealthy old merchant named Lovelorn lived. He had lost his wife, and his heart was still heavy with grief. To escape his loneliness, he married a young woman, the daughter of a poor shopkeeper.

The young woman, however, had no affection for the old man. She would often turn her back on him in bed and avoid his company. One night, while she was sleeping, a thief sneaked into the house. She was terrified and clung to the old man, thinking he was a protector.

The old man, surprised by her sudden affection, realized that she was hugging him out of fear of the thief. He smiled and said to the thief, "She usually shuns me, but now she's embracing me. Thank you for bringing us closer together. Take whatever you want."

The thief replied, "I want nothing here. But if I did want something, I would come back only when she does not cling to you like that." The old man realized that even a thief can be a benefactor if treated with kindness.

Foe-Crusher, the king, was advised by his counselors on how to deal with the situation. One counselor, Hook-Nose, suggested that the thief should not be killed. He explained, "We should expect help from our enemies if they are divided among themselves."

Moral: Even those who appear to be enemies can sometimes become benefactors if treated with kindness and understanding.

The Cave That Talked

In a dense forest, a hungry lion named Rough-Claw roamed around, searching for food. His throat was parched from thirst and hunger. As the sun began to set, he stumbled upon a massive cave and decided to hide inside.

Presently, the cave's owner, a sly jackal named Curd-Face, arrived at the entrance and started singing, "Cave ahoy! Cave aho-o-oy!" After a brief pause, he continued, "Hello! Don't you remember our agreement? You were supposed to speak to me when I returned, and I would greet you. But today, you're silent. I'll go to that other cave instead."

The lion thought, "This cave usually greets Curd-Face, but today it's quiet because it's afraid of me. I'll call out a greeting, and Curd-Face will follow the sound, providing me with food."

The lion loudly called out a greeting, but the cave's echo amplified the sound, scaring other forest creatures. Curd-Face, meanwhile, escaped, saying, "Joy comes from knowing what to dread, and sorrow strikes the foolish. I've lived in these woods for a long time, but never heard a cave talk."

Curd-Face departed, leaving the lion behind. The lion's plan had backfired.

A wise old crow named Live-Strong was overjoyed at Curd-Face's departure. He thought, "Red-Eye's escape is a blessing for us. He was wise, while the others were foolish. I can easily defeat them now."

Live-Strong started secretly building a woodpile at the fortress gate, planning to set it on fire and destroy the owls. The owls, blinded by their trust, didn't notice Live-Strong's sinister plan.

Cloudy, the king of the forest, was delighted when Live-Strong reported that the enemy's cave was ready to be burned. Cloudy and his followers, each carrying a lighted fagot, flew to the gate and threw the fire on Live-Strong's nest. The owls, trapped inside, could not find their way out of the flames.

Moral: Never trust an enemy, however friendly he seems, and do not make one without cause.

The Monkey and the Crocodile

A great rose-apple tree stood on the shore of the sea, its branches laden with fruit. Red-Face, a mischievous monkey, lived in the tree. One day, a crocodile named Ugly-Mug crawled out of the ocean and burrowed into the soft sand.

Red-Face welcomed the crocodile, offering him rose-apples and saying, "You're my guest, sir. Eat these delicious fruits, and we'll have a lovely conversation." The crocodile enjoyed the rose-apples and the conversation that followed.

When the crocodile returned home, he gave his wife the uneaten rose-apples. She asked him, "Where do you get these nectar fruits?" The crocodile replied, "I have a good friend, a monkey named Red-Face, who gives them to me."

His wife's eyes lit up with desire, and she said, "If you eat these fruits every day, your heart must be turned to nectar. Give me your friend's heart, and I'll eat it. Then I'll never grow old or sick, and I'll be a delightful companion for you."

The crocodile refused, explaining that Red-Face was like a brother to him. He couldn't kill him, especially since he gave them fruit. The crocodile's wife wouldn't give up, accusing him of loving Red-Face and spending all his time with her.

The crocodile was dejected, but he tried to reason with his wife. He said, "When I'm at your feet, why do you look at me with jealousy?" His wife's face swelled with tears, and she scolded him, saying, "You love Red-Face, don't you? His tricks have stolen your heart. My rivalry is futile, sir. Please abstain from this tricky game."

The crocodile visited Red-Face, telling him about his wife's demands. Red-Face was amused and said, "My friend, why have you not been here for so long? Why don't you speak cheerfully and tell a witty joke?" The crocodile said his wife had scolded him for not returning Red-Face's kindness. She wanted Red-Face to come home as a guest.

Red-Face suggested that the crocodile's wife come to the rose-apple tree, but the crocodile said, "My home is on a lovely sand-bank under the water. Climb on my back, and we'll travel comfortably." Red-Face agreed, but as they swam, he became terrified, thinking, "If I fall from his back, I'll drown."

The crocodile thought, "If he falls, he's doomed. I'll tell him my plan, and he can pray to his favorite god." He said, "Sir, I've deceived you, and you'll die because my wife ordered me to do it. Pray to your favorite god." Red-Face asked, "Why did you plan to kill me? What harm have I done your wife or you?"

The crocodile explained that his wife wanted to eat Red-Face's heart because she longed to taste the nectar fruits. Red-Face replied, "If that's the case, why didn't you tell me on shore? I have another heart, very sweet indeed, which I keep in a hole in the rose-apple tree."

The crocodile was delighted and said, "Give me that other heart, and my cross wife will eat it and give up starving herself. I'll take you back to the rose-apple tree." Red-Face laughed and scolded the crocodile, saying, "You fool! You traitor! How can anyone have two hearts? Go home, and never come back under the rose-apple tree."

The crocodile was embarrassed, thinking, "Oh, why was I such a fool as to tell him my plan? If I can win his confidence again, I'll do it." He said, "My friend, she has no need of a heart. What I said was just a joke to test your sentiments. Please come to our house as a guest. Your brother's wife is most eager for you."

Red-Face refused, saying, "Rascal! Go away this moment. I will not come. Tell Handsome, miss, that Theodore will see him in the well no more."

Moral: Those who trust a faithless friend are certain to fall into danger.

The Potter Militant

In a small village, a potter named Fight-Firm lived. One day, he rushed into a broken pot and fell, injuring his forehead. Although he was bleeding heavily, he struggled to get up.

Later, a severe famine hit the land, and Fight-Firm joined a group of guards to fight in another country. His bravery and strength earned him the king's attention.

The king noticed the ugly scar on Fight-Firm's forehead and thought he must be a great warrior. He gave him many honors and gifts, treating him like a prince. The other princes were jealous, but they kept quiet.

During a review of the army, the king asked Fight-Firm about his name, family, and the origin of his wound. Fight-Firm confessed that he was a potter who had gotten the scar from a broken pot when he was drunk.

The king was shocked and ashamed. He realized he had been fooled by Fight-Firm's story. He ordered his guards to punish Fight-Firm.

Fight-Firm asked the king not to punish him, but to let him prove his bravery in battle. The king refused. He said Fight-Firm might be brave and clever, but he had no noble blood. The king told him to leave before the soldiers learned he was a potter. So Fight-Firm left.

Moral: True worth is not measured by appearance or family background, but by one's actions and character.
